newsitem.title: USA: Hurricane Danny moves east toward Florida.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Danny moves east toward Florida.

text.p: Hurricane Danny weakened slightly as it moved inland from Mobile Bay on Saturday, but the storm continued to lash the U.S. coastline along the Gulf of Mexico with torrential rains and high winds.

At 8 p.m. EDT (0000 GMT), the National Weather Service said the eye of the hurricane was drifting eastward from Mobile Bay about 30 miles (48 km) southwest of Pensacola, Fla., with winds of 75 mph (120 kph), down from 80 mph (128 kph) on Saturday afternoon.

Although a minimal hurricane, Danny pummeled the Alabama coast with heavy rains and hurricane-force winds for more than 12 hours after drifting out of the Gulf and remaining nearly stationary near the mouth of Mobile Bay all day Saturday.
The storm smashed beachfront properties, stripped roofs and siding from buildings, downed trees and paralysed the bay area with widespread power outages.
"It's dumped a tremendous amount of rain on us," Baldwin County Emergency Management spokeswoman Leigh Anne Ryals said.
Alabama Gov. Fob James, who declared a state of emergency Friday, assured residents that he was ready to call out the National Guard and state police to help with the cleanup.
"I thought last night when I went to bed that we were seeing the end of this thing. Now it looks like it's only the beginning," James said.

Alabama residents in Mobile and Baldin counties continued to be deluged with rain. Downpours of 40 inches (101 cm) were recorded unofficially in some areas as flash floods swamped roads and low-lying areas.
About 1,500 people remained in Red Cross shelters in Alabama.
Hurricane warnings remained in effect from Gulfport, Miss., to Apalachicola, Fla., and forecasters worried that the storm could slip back over the Gulf and re-energise.
Tornado watches were in effect for the extreme southern areas of Mississippi and Alabama.
Danny was expected to be downgraded to a tropical storm if it maintained its inland course.

As violent winds and storm tides raked across the barrier islands of southern Alabama, a 120-foot (36.5 metre) car ferry tore loose from its moorings on Dauphin Island. The disappeared into the mouth of Mobile Bay, taking the pier along with it.

Winds downed 50 to 100 oak trees on the picturesque grounds of the antebellum Grand Hotel Resort in Point Clear, Ala., which juts out from the eastern shore of Mobile Bay. One was estimated to be 250 years old.
The storm has claimed one death. An Arizona man drowned in his swamped sailboat, which had broken up in heavy waves.
